## Why the deterministic model is kept

`magenta` carries a deterministic compartmental transmission model, an early
copy of the Imperial College malaria model with bed nets and indoor spraying,
written in [odin](https://mrc-ide.github.io/odin/) and shipped as
`inst/extdata/odin_itn_irs.R`. It does two jobs.

The first is small: the individual-based simulation does not model the
mosquito's response to nets and spraying itself, it reads a daily mosquito
death rate and feeding rate from the deterministic model's intervention block.
The second is the reason the model is kept at all. With no resistance and a
large population, the individual-based model should settle at the same
prevalence and incidence as the deterministic one for a given EIR, and
checking that it does is the quickest test that a change to the simulation has
not broken the transmission dynamics. `run_deterministic_model()` runs the
deterministic model from its equilibrium for a given setting and returns every
output through time, so that check is a few lines.

```{r setup}
library(magenta)
quiet <- housekeeping_list_create(quiet = TRUE, cluster = TRUE)
```

---

## Mosquito rates from coverage

The deterministic model's death rate `mu` and feeding rate `fv` depend only on
the net and spray coverage over time and the entomological parameters, not on
any state variable, so `pipeline()` evaluates that block directly with
`mu_fv_from_coverage()` instead of solving the whole model. It takes the
model parameter list and the yearly coverage vectors, and returns one row per
day:

```{r rates}
itn <- c(0, 0.3, 0.6, 0.6)
irs <- c(0, 0, 0.2, 0.2)
rates <- mu_fv_from_coverage(model_param_list_create(), ft = 0.4,
                             itn_cov = itn, irs_cov = irs, years = 4)
head(rates, 3)
```

Nets and spraying arrive on each anniversary and decay through the year, which
the rates show directly:

```{r rates-plot, fig.height = 4}
day <- seq_len(nrow(rates))
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plot(day, rates$mu, type = "l", ylab = "Mosquito death rate (mu)", xlab = "Day")
abline(v = 365 * 1:3, lty = 3)
plot(day, rates$fv, type = "l", ylab = "Feeding rate (fv)", xlab = "Day")
abline(v = 365 * 1:3, lty = 3)
```

The closed form is written in the same order of operations as the model's
generated code, so it is not an approximation: running the deterministic model
on the same inputs gives the same numbers to floating-point rounding
(identical on some platforms, within an ulp on others, depending on how the
generated C was compiled). The package tests assert this over every
configuration `pipeline()` can produce; here is one of them:

```{r rates-check}
det <- run_deterministic_model(EIR = 10, ft = 0.4, years = 4, itn_cov = itn,
                               irs_cov = irs, quiet = TRUE)
all.equal(rates$mu, det$mu, tolerance = 1e-12)
all.equal(rates$fv, det$fv, tolerance = 1e-12)
```

For a two-year seasonal run the closed form takes under a millisecond where the
solve took two seconds, which is why the model is no longer run inside
`pipeline()`.

---

## EIR to proportion infected and incidence

`run_deterministic_model()` starts at the model's equilibrium, so with no
interventions its outputs are flat and give the deterministic proportion
infected and clinical incidence for an EIR directly. The individual-based model
starts from the same equilibrium, approximated for a finite population, and
then does its own thing. The comparison below runs it at four EIRs for six
years with `N = 10000`, one replicate each, no resistance and 40% treatment
seeking, and records the proportion infected (`D + A + U + T`, all ages, with
no detection probability applied on either side) and the clinical incidence
per person per day. The simulation's loggers give the mean of each over the
year, so the individual-based values are year means; the deterministic value
is its flat equilibrium. The chunk takes about three minutes.

```{r sweep}
eirs <- c(1, 5, 20, 100)
N <- 10000
years <- 6
states <- c("S", "T", "D", "A", "U", "P")

deterministic <- t(sapply(eirs, function(e) {
  d <- run_deterministic_model(EIR = e, ft = 0.4, years = 1, quiet = TRUE)
  by_state <- sapply(states, function(st) d[[paste0(st, "out")]][365])
  c(infected = sum(by_state[c("D", "A", "U", "T")]), incidence = d$inc[365], by_state)
}))

ibm <- lapply(eirs, function(e) {
  sim <- pipeline(EIR = e, N = N, years = years, ft = 0.4, seed = 1L,
                  update_save = TRUE, update_length = 365, housekeeping_list = quiet)
  t(sapply(seq_len(years), function(i) {
    l <- sim[[i]]
    if (!is.null(l$Loggers)) l <- l$Loggers
    by_state <- sapply(states, function(st) l[[st]])
    c(infected = sum(by_state[c("D", "A", "U", "T")]), incidence = l$Incidence / N, by_state)
  }))
})
names(ibm) <- eirs
```

```{r sweep-table}
ibm_year <- function(what, i) sapply(ibm, function(x) x[i, what])
comparison <- data.frame(
  EIR = eirs,
  det_infected = round(deterministic[, "infected"], 3),
  ibm_year_1 = round(ibm_year("infected", 1), 3),
  ibm_year_3 = round(ibm_year("infected", 3), 3),
  ibm_year_6 = round(ibm_year("infected", years), 3),
  det_incidence = signif(deterministic[, "incidence"], 3),
  ibm_incidence_year_6 = signif(ibm_year("incidence", years), 3)
)
rownames(comparison) <- NULL
comparison
```

```{r sweep-plot, fig.height = 4.5}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
shades <- grey(seq(0.75, 0, length.out = years))
plot(eirs, deterministic[, "infected"], type = "b", log = "x", pch = 16,
     ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "EIR", ylab = "Proportion infected (D + A + U + T)",
     main = "Proportion infected")
for (i in seq_len(years)) {
  points(eirs, ibm_year("infected", i), pch = 17, col = shades[i])
}
legend("bottomright", bty = "n", pch = c(16, 17, 17), col = c("black", shades[1], shades[years]),
       legend = c("deterministic", "simulation, year 1", paste("simulation, year", years)))
plot(eirs, deterministic[, "incidence"], type = "b", log = "x", pch = 16,
     ylim = c(0, max(deterministic[, "incidence"]) * 1.3), xlab = "EIR",
     ylab = "Clinical incidence per person per day", main = "Incidence")
for (i in seq_len(years)) {
  points(eirs, ibm_year("incidence", i), pch = 17, col = shades[i])
}
```

Where the difference sits is clearer by compartment. The final year, each
model's proportion in each state:

```{r sweep-states}
by_state <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(eirs), function(k) {
  data.frame(
    EIR = eirs[k],
    model = c("deterministic", "simulation"),
    rbind(round(deterministic[k, states], 3), round(ibm[[k]][years, states], 3))
  )
}))
by_state
```

What holds, stated plainly. The two models agree on how the proportion
infected and the incidence scale with EIR. The simulation settles within about
three years and then stays flat, above the deterministic model at every EIR:
the excess is almost entirely in `A`, the asymptomatic state, with `U` below
the deterministic value at the higher EIRs and `S` lower to match. Clinical
incidence runs 10 to 25% under the deterministic value, most at EIR 100.
About two thirds of the gap is already there in year one. The same gap, of the
same size and in the same compartment, is present in magenta 1.3.7, so it is a
property of the two models as they stand rather than of the 1.4.0 changes.
Nothing here has been tuned to narrow it; it is recorded as an open finding in
the package's code review, and if a change to the simulation moves these
numbers that is worth knowing.

The deterministic model also reports a microscopy prevalence in under fives
(`prev`) and clinical incidence in under fives (`inc05`); the simulation's
`save_summary()` reports microscopy prevalence in 2 to 10 year olds
(`micro_2_10`). They are different age windows, so they are not compared here.
